newsitem.title: INDIA: India Congress rebels return to party fold.
newsitem.headline: India Congress rebels return to party fold.

text.p: A group of influential rebels decided on Wednesday to rejoin India's Congress party after a brief tie-up with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front, saying the nation needed a strong Congress to weather a crisis.
The All India Indira Congress (Tiwari) group said its merger with the parent body was not likely to change its support for Deve Gowda's tenuous alliance.

"This meeting unanimously resolves to integrate the All India Indira Congress (Tiwari) with the Indian National Congress without any conditions whatsoever," rebel party president Narayan Dutt Tiwari told a news conference in New Delhi.
Tiwari and another former minister, Arjun Singh, formed the breakaway group last year following deep differences with then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
Rao, who led the divided party to an historic defeat in general elections in April and May, resigned as party president in September and was replaced by Sitaram Kesri.
"Our decision to integrate with the Congress is an earnest effort to make Congress a predominant force in the country," Singh said at the joint news conference.
A party statement said its move to join hands with Kesri was prompted by a looming political crisis in India.
"The democratic polity bequeathed to us by the founding fathers of our constitution is itself in serious danger because of the ascendancy of communal, casteist and divisive forces," it said.
"The totally fractured mandate which emerged from the elections...is a cause for natural apprehension to all those who would like to see a united and strong India emerge," it said.
Kesri told Reuters he would formally respond to the merger move on Thursday.
Asked if the rebels' return responded to his call for party unity, Kesri said: "You know the direction in which I want to take the party. I will give my reaction towmorrow."

Both Kesri and the Tiwari-led rebels are close to Sonia Gandhi, the politically powerful but publicity-shy widow of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi. "We have not discussed the merger with Mrs Sonia Gandhi. But it falls within the ambit of her concern for deeper party unity," Singh said.
Deve Gowda assumed power at the head of a left-leaning alliance after the inconclusive polls. Congress agreed to support Deve Gowda but not join the government.

The breakaway Congress faction, which won four seats in the 545-member lower house, joined the 13-party coalition and won two ministerial posts. No decision had yet been taken on whether its two ministers would resign from the government, Singh said.
Asked if the move to return to Congress marked an end to the rebels' friendship with the United Front, Singh said: "We were not friends, we were partners in the alliance.
"There is no change in our stand about the alliance as the Congress is already supporting the government," Singh said.

The rebels' statement, issued after a general meeting of the Congress faction, said Kesri had "demonstrated that a sincere, determined and visionary effort is being made by him to redeem and renew the Indian National Congress in its true form".
They were due to meet Kesri later on Wednesday.
